table.title: EN · Long headers, short data
table.md:
| Region | Quarterly revenue (USD, millions) | Year-over-year growth rate | Number of active enterprise customers | Net promoter score |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| NA | 412.5 | 12% | 1,204 | 61 |
| EMEA | 287.1 | 9% | 986 | 58 |
| APAC | 198.4 | 21% | 640 | 64 |
| LATAM | 54.0 | 17% | 133 | 55 |

understanding.purpose: Compare regional revenue, growth, enterprise customer counts, and net promoter scores.
understanding.reading: Readers scan across each region to see its performance, then down each metric to compare regions. The long headers can occupy several lines while the short data rows remain compact.
groups: Revenue and year-over-year growth describe financial performance.
Enterprise customer count and net promoter score describe the customer base and its sentiment.
Region identifies each row and anchors comparisons across all four metrics.
keep_intact: Numeric values and their signs, decimal points, and digits
may_wrap: Header phrases at word spaces, including the revenue unit
Header words only in a tightly squeezed, no-scroll design

preferred.name: r3A
preferred.note: Combine r2B’s narrower revenue column with r2A’s growth width. This should preserve the four-line header while reducing overflow to 81px.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Give the financial headers more room than in compact-scroll while keeping the customer columns close to their word-width minimums. The 459px total aims for a more even header rhythm with less scrolling than r0B.

acceptable.name: r2A
acceptable.note: Widen growth from r1A while retaining its more economical revenue width. This should reduce the most disruptive header fragmentation with less scrolling than r1B.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Use the minimum content widths needed to keep the longest header words intact. This tests the shortest horizontal scroll that preserves whole words, accepting a taller header.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: Keep r1B’s more readable financial headers and trim the customer-count column slightly. This favors the first three columns visible on entry while keeping header words intact.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Retain r2A as the balanced reference: it gives the two financial columns equal width and avoids the extra growth line, with 87px of overflow.

bad.name: r1C
bad.note: Fit within 359px while giving Region enough room to keep region names intact. Distribute the remaining width among the metrics, accepting broken header words to keep all data visible at once.
bad.why: The headers visibly split words across lines, making them difficult to read and producing a header much taller than the data rows.

bad.name: r3C
bad.note: Fit all five columns within 359px while keeping the region column intact. This tests the cost of splitting long header words against the benefit of seeing every metric at once.
bad.why: The narrow columns visibly split several header words, while the seven-line header overwhelms the short data rows.

rationale: r3A keeps header words intact and gives all four data rows a compact, consistent rhythm. Its four-line header is easier to scan than the squeezed alternatives, while its 81px overflow costs less horizontal scrolling than the other four-line designs. The final metric still requires scrolling, but the first view includes nearly all of the enterprise-customer column.

general: Preserve recognizable words in headers when they explain the meaning of short data values.
Judge the whole table, including what a reader must scroll to reach, rather than optimizing height or width alone.
Give columns enough width for their content and role; equal widths are not inherently clearer.
specific: The long headers need substantially more space than the short values beneath them.
A modest horizontal scroll preserves readable headers and compact data rows at this viewport.

tradeoffs: r2B reduces overflow by 13px compared with r3A, but its growth-rate header takes five lines and makes the entire header taller. The wider four-line options provide slightly more horizontal space at the cost of additional scrolling.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates around r3A, not verified rendering thresholds; changes near a wrap boundary may alter the header rhythm. A designer prioritizing the smallest possible scroll could reasonably prefer r2B.

critique.good: The full table fits in the viewport, so all four metrics can be compared without horizontal scrolling. The short numeric rows are mostly compact.
critique.problems: The header dominates the table and is difficult to scan because several words break across lines. LATAM also breaks, making the last row taller and weakening the row rhythm.
critique.cause: At 65px, Region has only 44px for text, too little for both its header and LATAM. The metric columns provide only 44–61px of text width, forcing breaks inside long header words.

critique.good: Intact header words and uniformly compact data rows make the table much easier to read. Its four-line header is a reasonable compromise between height and width.
critique.problems: The viewport cuts through the customer-count column and leaves the promoter-score column offscreen, so readers must scroll to complete each regional comparison.
critique.cause: The first three columns use 276px, and the 110px customer column extends past the 360px viewport. The 477px table requires 117px of horizontal scrolling.

critique.good: The two-line headers are calm and easy to read, and the data rows retain a consistent rhythm.
critique.problems: The wide table separates the metrics and puts both customer measures beyond the initial viewport. Readers must scroll almost a full viewport to see the right edge, making across-row comparisons more cumbersome.
critique.cause: The 165px revenue, 145px growth, and 175px customer columns buy shorter headers at the cost of a 677px total width and 317px of overflow.

critique.good: Region names and values are easy to scan, and the compact body rows read as clear units. Header words remain intact.
critique.problems: The growth header is unusually tall and fragmented, giving it more visual weight than the other metrics. The promoter-score column lies beyond the initial viewport, so readers must scroll to complete each regional comparison.
critique.cause: The 82px growth column leaves 61px for text, forcing “Year-over-year” across three lines. The 434px total width puts the fifth column beyond the 360px viewport.

critique.good: The wider financial columns give the headers a calmer four-line rhythm, while region names and data remain intact. The body is compact and easy to compare down columns.
critique.problems: The initial view cuts through the customer-count column and leaves the promoter-score column off-screen. The extra width improves the header but increases the distance needed to see all metrics.
critique.cause: The 105px revenue and 95px growth widths reduce wrapping, but together with the other columns they produce a 460px table.

critique.good: All four metrics are visible together without horizontal scrolling, and the compact data rows support comparisons across regions.
critique.problems: The header is much taller than the body and is difficult to scan: several words break into small fragments, obscuring the metric names. This visual fragmentation outweighs the benefit of seeing the whole table at once.
critique.cause: The metric columns leave only 47–57px for text after padding and borders, less than the width of several header words. The reported zero mid-word splits does not match the visible render.

critique.good: The four-line header establishes a consistent rhythm, and the short data rows remain easy to scan. Header words and regional labels stay intact.
critique.problems: The customer-count column is cut by the initial viewport, and the final metric requires sideways scrolling. The revenue header has a cramped unit, although its column uses nearly as much width as growth.
critique.cause: The 447px total exceeds the viewport by 87px. At 95px, revenue has 74px of text space, so its unit wraps across two lines.

critique.good: This is the narrowest scrolling design, and it keeps header words intact while bringing more of the customer-count column into view.
critique.problems: The growth header becomes a conspicuous five-line stack, making the entire header row taller and weakening its relationship with revenue. The final metric still requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 82px growth column leaves 61px for text, causing “year-over-year” to wrap at its hyphens across three lines. Reducing revenue to 89px saves space but does not offset that extra header line.

critique.good: The four-line header and compact data rows retain the readable rhythm of r2A. The wider revenue column gives its header more room.
critique.problems: The additional revenue width produces no reduction in overall header height, while the viewport cuts further into the customer-count column. The final metric is farther away.
critique.cause: Increasing revenue to 105px raises the total width to 457px, but the 97px customer-count column still requires four header lines.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_equal.why: All five columns fit, but several headers break within words, making the tall header difficult to scan.

ref_auto.why: The first four columns are readable and the headers mostly wrap at word boundaries, but the final metric requires horizontal scrolling.

r1B.why: The headers are readable, but the viewport cuts through the enterprise-customer column, obscuring part of a metric that readers may want to compare.

r3A.why: Four complete columns fit in the viewport, with readable headers and compact rows; the promoter score requires scrolling.

r2A.why: Four complete columns fit, and the headers wrap cleanly. The promoter score lies beyond the initial view.

r1C.why: The whole table fits, but repeated word breaks in the headers make the columns hard to identify and create a very tall header.

raw.unsure: The supplied images do not show the full offscreen portions of B–E, so the widths and readability of their final columns cannot be assessed completely.

r3A.why: Headers wrap at sensible word boundaries, and the visible values form clear rows. The fifth column requires horizontal scrolling.

r1C.why: All columns fit, but headers break inside many words, making them difficult to read and creating an excessively tall header.

r2A.why: The first four columns have readable headers and well-aligned values. The fifth column lies mostly beyond the viewport and requires scrolling.

r1B.why: The headers wrap cleanly, but the viewport cuts through the customer column, so readers must scroll to see its values and the final column.

ref_auto.why: Four columns and their values fit in the viewport, with mostly natural header breaks. The final column still requires scrolling, and the growth header is relatively tall.

ref_equal.why: The full table fits, but numerous breaks inside header words make the column labels hard to decipher.

raw.unsure: A and C appear nearly identical at the visible scale, and the screenshots do not clearly show the full extent of their final columns. E shows slightly more of the final column but uses an extra line in the growth header.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
